days.title: Ollama & API
days.summary: Start the local model service, confirm the model id is lfm3, and define token and context window in your own words. First run may take 45–60 min while lfm3 downloads; later sittings are ~30 min.

steps.title: Why Day 1 — bootstrap the runtime
steps.body:
Ollama is a program on your machine. It loads a model and answers HTTP calls. It is not the chat UI and not model training.

Two URLs share port 11434:
1) GET /api/tags — is the process up, and which model names are installed?
2) POST /v1/chat/completions — the chat call you use from Day 2. Base URL for that family: http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1

The model id in JSON this week is lfm3. Read “The two URLs” and “How the seven days fit,” then run the exercises.

Useful distinction: connection refused means nothing is listening (run ./server.sh). model not found means the name in JSON does not match ollama list—not a bad prompt.
steps.why: When a later call fails, check port 11434 and the model string before editing prompts.
steps.figureAlt: Ollama on port 11434 exposes an inventory URL and a chat URL.

steps.title: Exercise — start the LLM service
steps.body:
Run from the repo root (folder that contains server.sh):

./server.sh starts Ollama if port 11434 is closed, pulls lfm3 the first time (can take many minutes), and sends one short warm-up request.

Success: a banner with API base http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 and model id lfm3. If ollama is not on PATH, install from ollama.com. On Windows, use Git Bash/WSL or bash scripts/server.sh.

Optional: ollama run lfm3 and ask one question before Day 2’s HTTP exercise.
steps.why: One command is the session habit. Remembering serve, pull, and a warm-up curl separately is how people skip a step and then debug the wrong layer.
steps.outcome: The terminal banner shows port 11434 and model lfm3. A first-time pull finishing counts as success.
steps.figureAlt: server.sh starts Ollama, pulls lfm3 if needed, then warms the model.

steps.title: Exercise — verify model name
steps.body:
ollama list prints a table. For JSON, use the NAME column only.

Example: a row lfm3:latest still maps to "model": "lfm3" in this lab unless your list shows a different name.

Size and modified columns are not sent in requests. If lfm3 is missing, ./server.sh did not finish pulling—run it again.

Tomorrow’s curls use "model": "lfm3". A mismatch returns model not found (name error, not content error).
steps.why: The string in JSON is not a description of the model. It is an exact lookup key.
steps.outcome: You can point at the NAME cell you will paste into Day 2.
steps.figureAlt: Copy the NAME column into the model field. lfm3:latest is still requested as lfm3.

steps.title: Exercise — health via /api/tags
steps.body:
Run the curls below, then pick the answer that matches what you saw.

This request does not call the model—it lists installed models.
steps.why: /api/tags is Ollama’s own inventory. /v1/chat/completions is the chat API on the same port. Day 2 uses the second one. Today you only prove the first.
commands: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print('models:', [m.get('name') for m in d.get('models',[])][:5])"
steps.outcome: You see a models array, not connection refused, and you can name one model.
steps.figureAlt: Success is JSON with a models array; connection refused means Ollama is down.

submissionQuestions.label: After GET /api/tags, which outcome did you get?

options.label: JSON with a models array (each item has a name)
curl: connection refused — no JSON body
A chat completion with message.content from the model
An HTML 404 page from a web browser
HTTP 200 with an empty body and no JSON

steps.title: Reflect — define token (journal)
steps.body: Read “A token” in the chapter, then answer each multiple-choice question and **Save locally**.
steps.why: Tokens drive billing, speed, and context limits in every product.
steps.outcome: Journal answers: subword pieces; usage.prompt_tokens / completion_tokens.
steps.figureAlt: Hello may be one token or several. Counts live in usage, not in the word.

options.label: A subword piece the tokenizer passes to the model—not always one English word
Always exactly one keyboard character
Always one dictionary word
One raw byte from the UTF-8 file on disk
One pixel in a rendered screenshot of the prompt

submissionQuestions.label: Why can “Hello” be more than one token?

options.label: Tokenizers can split subwords; a leading space is often its own token
It cannot—Hello is always exactly one token
The model randomly decides how many tokens to use
curl merges multiple words into one token automatically
GPU drivers combine letters into one token for speed

submissionQuestions.label: Which fields report token counts in the chat JSON (from Day 2)?

options.label: usage.prompt_tokens and usage.completion_tokens (plus usage.total_tokens)
choices[0].length and choices[0].width
model.size and model.modified from ollama list
HTTP Content-Length headers only
finish_reason only—no token counts exist

steps.title: Reflect — define context window (journal)
steps.body: Read “The context budget,” then answer the multiple-choice questions and **Save locally**.
steps.why: Day 5 will make this limit visible. Phase 2 exists because the limit does not go away when the documents get bigger.
steps.outcome: Journal mentions prompt + reply share one limit; overflow truncates or errors.
steps.figureAlt: One call shares about 4096 tokens between what you send and the reply.

submissionQuestions.label: What must fit inside one chat/completions call?

options.label: Your messages (system/user/history you send) and the model’s new reply—including reasoning
Only the latest user message—replies are unlimited
Only the model reply—prompts do not count
The entire model weights file on disk
Nothing—context is unlimited on localhost

submissionQuestions.label: Someone pastes a whole PDF into one user message. What is realistic?

options.label: Often truncate, error, or cut off—the model may not see all pages
The model always reads every page with no limit
Ollama automatically enables RAG and indexes the PDF
The API splits the PDF across unlimited free calls automatically
PDF text is ignored; only the filename is used

submissionQuestions.label: Why ~4096 tokens as a working cap in this lab?

options.label: A shared teaching ruler so everyone’s exercises stay comparable
It is the exact hardware RAM size of your GPU in bytes
It is a legal maximum enforced by OpenAI globally
You must measure it with curl on Day 1 before continuing
It equals the maximum PDF page count Ollama supports

steps.title: Close out
steps.body: Close-out check: pick the best answer for each item, **Save locally**, then mark the step done.
steps.why: Day 2 sends a real chat request. It assumes you already know the URL, the model id, and what the token fields mean.
steps.outcome: You can say the four lines without the chapter open. Day 1 then shows Done.

submissionQuestions.label: Where do chat requests go in this lab?

options.label: POST http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/chat/completions (base http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1)
POST http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags with a user message
https://api.openai.com only—local Ollama has no chat URL
POST requests to github.com/farnodes/AILab
https://ollama.com/chat for all local models

submissionQuestions.label: Which model id do you send in JSON this week?

options.label: lfm3 (from ollama list NAME column in this lab)
lfm3:latest including the tag every time
Any display name you remember—no need to match the list
gpt-4o
The SIZE column from ollama list
Subword pieces; counts in usage.prompt_tokens and usage.completion_tokens
Always one token per English word; no usage block exists
Character count in message.content only
Reasoning tokens are free and not in usage
Token counts come from GET /api/tags
One shared budget (~4096 here) for prompt + reply in that call
Prompt unlimited; only replies are capped
Separate windows—4096 for you and 4096 for the model
The server remembers all past curls without resending history
A full PDF in one message always fits if you use lfm3

days.title: Chat JSON
days.summary: Send one chat request, save the JSON, and read content, reasoning, usage, and finish_reason.

steps.title: Why Day 2 — one-shot chat JSON
steps.body:
A batch job sends one POST and stores one JSON object. That is non-streaming chat: omit stream, or set it false.

Today you send a real prompt, save the full response, and read four things: message.content (what a user would see), message.reasoning (LFM3’s hidden thinking), usage (token counts), and finish_reason (why it stopped).

Read “One chat request” and “Reading the response,” then run ./server.sh.
steps.why: Batch + tests use one JSON body; streaming comes later for interactive UX.

steps.title: Learn — request contract
steps.body:
A request needs model and messages. Each message has a role and content.

1) system — rules (optional today)
2) user — the task
3) assistant — an earlier reply, only if you want the next turn to remember it

Sketch that shape on paper or in the journal without looking at curl. The chapter section “One chat request” is the answer key.
steps.why: Every SDK ultimately sends this shape.
steps.outcome: You can write model, messages, and the three roles without the chapter open.
steps.figureAlt: One JSON request in, four fields to read on the way out.

steps.title: Exercise — realistic one-shot prompt
steps.body: Scenario: Classify urgency of a user message (practice for later agent routing).
steps.why: More memorable than Hello—and still one user message.
commands: -d '{"model":"lfm3","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"User message: \"Server down since 9am.\" Reply with one word: urgent or normal."}]}' | python3 -m json.tool
steps.outcome: Single JSON object; choices[0].message.content is non-empty.

steps.title: Exercise — save artifact
steps.body: Save the Hello response (simpler baseline) for diffing in later days.
steps.why: Files beat terminal scrollback for learning and git.
steps.outcome: examples/day02-response.json exists and is valid JSON.

steps.title: Exercise — extract user-visible answer
steps.body: Scenario: Your app only displays message.content to the user.
steps.why: Other fields are metadata or hidden reasoning.
steps.outcome: You see the assistant greeting without reading raw JSON by hand.

steps.title: Exercise — LFM3 reasoning cost
steps.body: Scenario: Latency and token bills include reasoning tokens even if the UI hides them.
steps.why: Short content + long reasoning is normal on LFM3.
commands: python3 -c "import json; d=json.load(open('examples/day02-response.json')); m=d['choices'][0]['message']; r=m.get('reasoning',''); print('content chars', len(m.get('content',''))); print('reasoning chars', len(r)); print('reasoning preview:', r[:120])"
steps.outcome: You notice reasoning often dominates completion_tokens.

steps.title: Exercise — usage & finish_reason
steps.body:
Run the command above, then in your journal write a short bullet list:
• prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens (copy numbers from output)
• finish_reason and what it implies for this Hello call
• One sentence: why completion_tokens can exceed visible content length on LFM3
steps.why: stop = OK; length = need shorter prompt or higher max_tokens.
commands: python3 -c "import json; d=json.load(open('examples/day02-response.json')); c=d['choices'][0]; u=d.get('usage',{}); print('finish_reason:', c.get('finish_reason')); print('usage:', u)"
steps.outcome: Journal lists prompt/completion/total tokens and finish_reason stop.
steps.journalGuide:
The usage block is how backend jobs prove cost and health. prompt_tokens counts the input side (all roles in messages[]). completion_tokens counts generated tokens—including reasoning tokens on LFM3 even when the UI only shows message.content. total_tokens is the sum.

finish_reason tells you why generation stopped: stop usually means the model ended naturally; length means it hit max_tokens or the context ceiling—your prompt or answer may be truncated. Dashboards alert on length spikes because they often mean bad UX or runaway spend.

Journaling these fields now builds a habit: when something “looks wrong,” you check JSON metadata before rewriting the prompt.

steps.title: Exercise — stateless multi-turn
steps.body: The server forgets every curl. This request sends the memory itself: user says a name, assistant greets them, user asks for the name. If the reply is Sam, history worked because you sent it, not because Ollama remembered.
steps.why: Multi-turn chat is your app resending messages, not a session on the server.
commands: -d '{"model":"lfm3","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"My name is Sam."},{"role":"assistant","content":"Hi Sam."},{"role":"user","content":"What name did I give? One word."}]}' \
steps.outcome: Model answers Sam (proves history is only what you send).

steps.title: Close out
steps.body:
Confirm examples/day02-response.json exists. In your journal write 2–4 sentences:
When would you pick non-streaming? When streaming? Name one example product surface for each (e.g. nightly ticket classifier vs in-app chat).
steps.why: Day 3 is streaming on the same endpoint.
steps.outcome: Day 2 complete in sidebar.
steps.journalGuide:
Non-streaming (stream false or omitted) waits until the full JSON object is ready. That is ideal for batch jobs, tests, and pipelines that store one record per request—your Day 2 artifact is the pattern.

Streaming (stream true) sends many SSE chunks so a UI can paint text incrementally. The same messages and model are used; only the transport changes. Choose stream for interactive products; choose batch when you need a single parsed object and do not care about time-to-first-token.

Neither mode remembers prior curls—multi-turn only works if your app resends history in messages[].

days.title: Streaming
days.summary: Stream the same endpoint, measure time to the first byte, and join only the visible text.

steps.title: Why Day 3 — streaming for interactive UX
steps.body:
Scenario: A chat product shows tokens as they arrive so users know the model is working. Same endpoint as Day 2, but stream:true and SSE chunks.

Today you measure TTFT, parse delta.reasoning vs delta.content on LFM3, and save examples/day03-streaming.txt for Day 7.

Run ./server.sh.
steps.why: Perceived speed = time to first token, not time to full JSON.

steps.title: Learn — batch vs stream
steps.body:
Same URL and same messages as Day 2. Add "stream": true.

The response is many lines that start with data:, then a final data: [DONE]. Visible words arrive in delta.content. LFM3 often sends delta.reasoning first.

Read the sample lines in the chapter section “Streaming” before you run curl. You should be able to name one way this HTTP body differs from Day 2’s single JSON object.
steps.why: Choose stream for UI; batch for tests and ETL.
steps.outcome: You can name one field that differs in the HTTP response shape.
steps.figureAlt: A stream is reasoning, then content, then finish_reason, then DONE.

steps.title: Exercise — live stream (product-style prompt)
steps.body: Scenario: User asks for a short list—watch tokens appear incrementally.
steps.why: curl -N disables buffering so you feel TTFT.
commands: -d '{"model":"lfm3","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"List three tips for learning APIs. Number them."}],"stream":true}'
steps.outcome: You see multiple data: lines before [DONE].

steps.title: Learn — wire format
steps.body:
From the live stream, copy one data: line into your notes. Mark which of these it updated:
1) delta.reasoning
2) delta.content
3) finish_reason

Match it to the sample in “Streaming.” Your Phase 1 client will concatenate delta.content and ignore the rest when drawing the bubble.
steps.why: Your Phase 1 client will concatenate delta fields.
steps.outcome: You can point to delta.content vs delta.reasoning in a chunk.

steps.title: Exercise — measure TTFT
steps.body:
The number printed is seconds until the first byte (curl’s time_starttransfer). That is your time-to-first-token stand-in.

Write it in examples/day03-streaming.txt on the next step, and one journal paragraph: the number, whether you expect the first chunk to be reasoning or content on LFM3, and why a chat UI cares.
steps.why: On LFM3 the first byte is often reasoning, so a fast TTFT can still mean a blank chat bubble.
steps.outcome: You have one number in seconds for time to first byte, written down.
steps.journalGuide:
The number from curl is seconds until the first byte (time_starttransfer). That is your stand-in for time to first token: delay until the first data: chunk. Users perceive speed from that delay more than from the time until the stream finishes. SLO dashboards often track TTFT separately from total latency.

On LFM3 the first chunks may be delta.reasoning, not user-visible delta.content. That means TTFT can look “fast” while the user still waits for readable text—product teams need to decide whether to show reasoning, hide it, or show a spinner until content starts.

Record TTFT in two places: a durable examples/day03-streaming.txt (artifact) and your journal (interpretation). Numbers without interpretation do not survive a week.

steps.title: Exercise — rebuild answer from chunks
steps.body: Scenario: Your CLI must print only user-visible text from a stream.
steps.why: Teaches parsing without a framework.
commands:
| python3 -c "import sys,json; out=[]
for line in sys.stdin:
  line=line.strip()
  if not line.startswith('data:') or line=='data: [DONE]': continue
  d=json.loads(line[6:])
  c=d['choices'][0].get('delta',{}).get('content') or ''
  out.append(c)
  sys.stdout.write(c)
print(); print('--- joined:', ''.join(out))"
steps.outcome: Joined text matches what you saw stream (e.g. 1…5).

steps.title: Exercise — save learning note
steps.body: Capture TTFT, model, and whether reasoning preceded content.
steps.why: Day 7 review uses this artifact.
commands:
printf 'Day 3
TTFT seconds: (fill in)
Model: lfm3
Note: reasoning chunks before content? yes/no
' > examples/day03-streaming.txt
steps.outcome: File exists with your TTFT filled in.

steps.title: Exercise — final chunk
steps.body: Scenario: Client must detect normal completion vs truncation.
steps.why: finish_reason on last chunk matches Day 2 semantics.
steps.outcome: You see finish_reason stop (or length) before [DONE].

steps.title: Close out
steps.body: Journal 3–5 sentences: For the capstone track you are leaning toward (even if not chosen until Day 6), which flows would be streaming vs batch? Mention one risk for each choice.
steps.why: Day 4 tunes prompts, not transport.
steps.outcome: Day 3 complete.
steps.journalGuide:
Streaming is not “better”—it is appropriate when a human waits on the screen. Batch is appropriate when a worker processes a queue and writes to a database. Your capstone will likely use both: stream for demos and admin chat, batch for indexing, evals, and cron jobs.

Tie the choice to failure modes: streams need parsers, reconnect logic, and partial UI state; batch needs timeouts and memory for large JSON bodies.

days.title: Sampling preview
days.summary: Ask the same question twice: a strict low-temperature bot and a warmer coach.

steps.title: Why Day 4 — steer behavior without changing models
steps.body:
Scenario: Same lfm3 powers a terse status bot and a friendly onboarding coach—system prompt + temperature do the work.

Today you run the same user question under two profiles, save JSON, compare tokens and tone.

Run ./server.sh.
steps.why: Cheaper than fine-tuning for style and format constraints.

steps.title: Learn — system + user roles
steps.body:
Both profiles use the same user question. Only the policy changes.

system — how to answer (length, tone, format)
user — what to answer

temperature 0 asks for a steadier wording. temperature 1 allows more variation and usually more tokens.

Write one system line you could reuse, 20 words or fewer, such as “Reply in at most 15 words. No preamble.” Read “Steering without a new model” if the split between roles is unclear.
steps.why: Misplacing instructions in user text weakens control.
steps.outcome: You can write a one-line system rule for “JSON only” or “max 15 words”.
steps.figureAlt: Same question, two policies: a short bot and a warmer coach.

steps.title: Exercise — support bot (temp 0)
steps.body: Scenario: Incident bot must be short and deterministic.
steps.why: temperature 0 + strict system reduces variance.
commands: -d '{"model":"lfm3","temperature":0,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Reply in at most 15 words. No preamble."},{"role":"user","content":"Explain what a token is in one sentence."}]}' \
steps.outcome: day04-terse.json saved; content is noticeably short.

steps.title: Exercise — onboarding coach (temp 1)
steps.body: Scenario: Teaching mode allows warmth and extra context.
steps.why: Higher temperature adds variation run-to-run.
commands: -d '{"model":"lfm3","temperature":1,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Be friendly and thorough; use two short paragraphs."},{"role":"user","content":"Explain what a token is in one sentence."}]}' \
steps.outcome: day04-verbose.json saved; completion_tokens usually higher.

steps.title: Exercise — compare outputs
steps.body:
After running the compare command, add a small table in your journal:
Columns: Profile (terse / verbose) | completion_tokens | tone (1 line) | good for (product surface)
One closing sentence: which profile you would ship for an incident bot vs a learning coach.
steps.why: Quantitative + qualitative beats gut feel.
commands: python3 -c "import json; t=json.load(open('examples/day04-terse.json')); v=json.load(open('examples/day04-verbose.json')); print('TERSE tokens', t['usage'].get('completion_tokens')); print('VERBOSE tokens', v['usage'].get('completion_tokens')); print('---'); print('TERSE:', t['choices'][0]['message']['content']); print('VERBOSE:', v['choices'][0]['message']['content'][:300])"
steps.outcome: Journal table: tokens, tone, which profile for which product surface.
steps.journalGuide:
Same model, same user question, different system prompt and temperature—two product surfaces. Temperature near 0 reduces randomness: good for support bots, extraction, and “same input → same shape output.” Temperature 1 allows more variation: better for brainstorming coaches, marketing drafts, and creative onboarding—at the cost of higher completion_tokens and less predictability.

When you journal, combine numbers and taste: token counts explain cost; tone explains user trust. A terse bot that saves tokens but confuses users is not a win.

steps.title: Reflect — when to use which
steps.body:
Write three bullets in your journal:
1) A feature that should use temperature 0 (name the user and failure if it drifts)
2) A feature that benefits from temperature 1
3) One system prompt rule you will reuse in Phase 2 (exact wording, ≤20 words)
steps.why: Phase 1 covers Top-P and LFM3-specific tuning.
steps.outcome: Concrete examples tied to your capstone track.
steps.journalGuide:
Temperature and system prompts are the cheapest knobs before fine-tuning. temp 0 + strict system rules fit structured, high-stakes outputs (status, JSON, compliance). temp 1 + permissive system fit exploration and teaching.

System rules you write now become templates in Phase 2 (“answer only from provided context”, “cite chunk ids”, “refuse if not in docs”). Pick one rule you expect to reuse so you are not inventing policy from scratch later.

steps.title: Close out
steps.body: Both JSON files exist. Mark day done.
steps.why: Day 5 explores limits of stuffing text into one call.
steps.outcome: Day 4 complete.

days.title: Context limit
days.summary: Compare a tiny prompt with an oversized one so the context limit is something you saw.

steps.title: Why Day 5 — context is a hard budget
steps.body:
One call has one token budget. It must hold the messages you send and the reply, including reasoning. This lab uses about 4096 tokens as the working cap.

The stress test is built so you can see a miss: the question is at the start, junk fills the middle, and the word MAGICEND is only at the end. If the model does not say MAGICEND, it did not reliably see the tail.

Read “The context budget,” then run ./server.sh. A small control call comes before the long one.
steps.why: Phase 2 RAG sends chunks instead of megabytes in one shot.

steps.title: Exercise — baseline small request
steps.body: Confirm normal stop + usage on a tiny prompt before stress test.
steps.why: You need a control to compare against failure.
steps.outcome: finish_reason stop with modest token counts.

steps.title: Exercise — build oversized prompt
steps.body:
The file is three parts on purpose:
1) A question at the start: what is the magic word at the end?
2) The word “word” repeated, so the middle is long and useless
3) The suffix MAGICEND, which is the right answer only if the model still sees the tail

Check the byte size with wc. You are not trying to craft a good prompt. You are trying to overflow a bad one.
steps.why: Tests whether early instructions survive (often they do not).
commands: python3 -c "prefix='What is the magic word at the end of this text? Reply one word. '; filler='word '*3000; suffix=' MAGICEND'; open('examples/day05-long-prompt.txt','w').write(prefix+filler+suffix)"
steps.outcome: File size printed; you know MAGICEND is the correct answer if model reads the tail.

steps.title: Exercise — send long prompt
steps.body:
In your journal, under “Day 5 — long prompt”, write:
• Result: JSON saved OR error saved (filename)
• One line on what you expect happened inside the model/runtime
steps.why: Real systems hit this in production with big PDF pastes.
commands:
python3 << 'PY'
import json, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path
text = Path('examples/day05-long-prompt.txt').read_text()
body = json.dumps({'model': 'lfm3', 'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': text}]}).encode()
req = urllib.request.Request('http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/chat/completions', data=body, headers={'Content-Type': 'application/json'})
try:
    r = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120)
    Path('examples/day05-long-response.json').write_bytes(r.read())
    print('saved examples/day05-long-response.json')
except Exception as e:
    Path('examples/day05-long-error.txt').write_text(str(e))
    print('error saved to examples/day05-long-error.txt')
PY
steps.outcome: You have either JSON or error file—journal which.
steps.journalGuide:
This step either succeeds with a large JSON response or fails with an HTTP/client error—both are valid learning outcomes. Production systems see both daily. Your journal must record which path happened so future-you knows which artifact to open.

If saved: note finish_reason and whether the answer matched MAGICEND. If error: paste the error class/message and estimate whether the prompt was likely over the context budget.

steps.title: Reflect — what happened?
steps.body:
Answer in plain language in your journal:
1) Did the model return MAGICEND (or close)?
2) What was finish_reason?
3) If error, what did the message say?
4) In one sentence, how does this connect to the context window you defined on Day 1?
steps.why: Your capstone RAG design should avoid this failure mode.
steps.outcome: Journal answers all four questions in plain language.
steps.journalGuide:
Long prompts test “lost in the middle”: instructions at the start and facts at the end may not both survive when filler consumes the budget. MAGICEND at the tail is deliberate—if the model answers something else, it likely never attended to the end.

finish_reason length often means generation hit a cap—not necessarily that the input fit. Errors may mean the server refused oversize input. Relate what you saw to ~4096 tokens as a mental model, not magic.

steps.title: Reflect — mitigation
steps.body:
Write one paragraph: chunking and retrieval send a few relevant pieces instead of the whole document. Name what still has to fit in the same budget afterward: system rules, the chunks you kept, the question, and the answer.

The chapter section “The context budget” states the same idea in short form. Use your Day 5 result as the example.
steps.why: Connects bootstrap pain to curriculum arc.
steps.outcome: You can explain RAG’s purpose without buzzwords.
steps.journalGuide:
RAG is not a buzzword—it is an engineering response to context limits. Instead of one megabyte user message, you chunk documents, embed chunks, retrieve top-k relevant pieces, and inject only those into messages[]. The model then answers from a small evidence set.

Chunking strategy (size, overlap), embedding model choice, and retrieval quality all matter as much as the LLM call. Phase 2 walks those pieces; today you journal the motivation so Phase 2 feels necessary, not optional.

steps.title: Close out
steps.body: Mark done. You have felt context limits, not just read about them.
steps.why: Day 6 picks direction for the rest of the lab.
steps.outcome: Day 5 complete.

days.title: Roadmap & capstone
days.summary: Choose a capstone and name the first technique you will try before adding more tools.

steps.title: Why Day 6 — connect skills to a capstone
steps.body:
Scenario: Phase 0 taught the wire protocol; Phase 1–5 teach depth. Without a chosen outcome, daily exercises feel random.

Today you pick a capstone track and map Phase 1–2 skills to it using ROADMAP’s Decide first table.
steps.why: Purpose improves retention more than extra curl.

steps.title: Exercise — Decide first table
steps.body:
In ROADMAP, the “Decide first” table says what to try before fine-tuning or a free-roaming agent:
1) Facts from docs → retrieval
2) Reliable JSON → a schema, then a prompt example
3) A new capability → a tool
4) A business process → a workflow
5) IDE behavior → rules and skills

In the journal write: “Decide first: for [your need], I will try [that row] first because …” in 2–3 sentences.
steps.why: Teams retrieve before fine-tune; workflows before full autonomy.
steps.outcome: Journal cites one row from the table with your project in mind.
steps.journalGuide:
ROADMAP’s “Decide first” table is a prioritization guardrail. Teams often jump to fine-tuning or agents when retrieval or a simple workflow would ship faster. Reading the table with your capstone in mind forces a explicit bet: which column matches your first user value?

Quote or paraphrase one row: need (facts, JSON, tools, process) → first technique to try. That sentence becomes your north star when Phase 1–2 offer many shiny options.

steps.title: Exercise — pick capstone track
steps.body:
Pick one track and put it in the journal header: “Capstone track: …”.
1) Dev platform — tools, editor, codegen
2) Knowledge product — search, citations, retrieval
3) Automation — workflows, scheduled jobs, integrations
4) Learning lab — extend this repo and write up what you try

Add one sentence on why it fits work you actually do or want to do. You can change tracks at a phase boundary. You cannot learn well with no track.
steps.why: Default choice beats endless debate.
steps.outcome: One track name written in journal header.
steps.journalGuide:
A capstone track is a label for scope, not a contract. Dev platform = tools, IDE, codegen; Knowledge product = RAG, citations, search; Automation = workflows, cron, integrations; Learning lab = extend this repo and document experiments.

Pick one for the next weeks—you can change it at Phase boundaries, but indecision wastes daily 30-minute blocks. Write the track name where future-you will see it (journal header or PROGRESS table).

steps.title: Exercise — three bullets + phase map
steps.body:
Journal exactly four bullets:
1) Capstone in one sentence
2) Phase 1 unlocks … (specific, not generic)
3) Phase 2 unlocks …
4) Biggest risk if you skip fundamentals
steps.why: Four bullets still fit 30 minutes if you stay terse.
steps.outcome: Journal entry you can reread before Day 8.
steps.journalGuide:
Four bullets connect Phase 0 skills to Phase 1–2 depth. Phase 1 (SLMs, quantization, clients) explains how lfm3 runs locally and how your code calls it. Phase 2 (RAG) explains how to give models facts without infinite context. Naming “biggest risk” early prevents fantasy architectures.

This entry is what you reread on Day 8 when GGUF and memory math feel abstract—tie every Phase 1 topic back to the capstone sentence.

steps.title: Learn — what Day 8 starts
steps.body: Phase 1 Day 8: GGUF & quantization—how lfm3 fits in memory and on disk.
steps.why: Sets expectation after bootstrap.
steps.outcome: You know the next technical topic after Phase 0.

steps.title: Close out
steps.body: Mark done. Day 7 is timed review of Days 2–3.
steps.why: Muscle memory before quantization math.
steps.outcome: Day 6 complete.

days.title: Phase 0 review
days.summary: Demo a batch call and a stream from memory, then score the Phase 0 checklist.

steps.title: Why Day 7 — prove bootstrap skills
steps.body:
Scenario: You join a pairing session and must demo local inference in five minutes without docs.

Today you time yourself on batch + stream flows and self-score Phase 0 exit criteria.
steps.why: If this is hard, repeat weak days before Phase 1.

steps.title: Timed demo — batch chat (< 5 min)
steps.body: From memory: POST Hello, print content only.
steps.why: Mirrors Day 2 integration path.
steps.outcome: Completed under 5 minutes including server check.

steps.title: Timed demo — stream (< 5 min)
steps.body: stream:true, -N, show last lines include [DONE].
steps.why: Mirrors Day 3 product path.
steps.outcome: You see data: lines and [DONE].

steps.title: Self-check — exit rubric
steps.body:
Close the chapter. Say each term once out loud, then make a journal table:
Concept | yes / partial / no | one-line proof
Rows: token, context window, stream vs batch, base URL, model id.

Partial or no means redo that day before Day 8. The bar is in “What Day 7 should sound like.”
steps.why: Matches phase0 exit criteria.
steps.outcome: At least four yes; re-study any partial.
steps.journalGuide:
Phase 0 exit criteria are operational, not academic. You should be able to explain token, context window, stream vs batch, base URL, and model id without opening docs—because on-call and pairing sessions do not wait for grep.

Self-grade honestly: “partial” means repeat the weak day before Phase 1. Journal yes/partial/no creates a checklist you can paste into PROGRESS.md when you mark Phase 0 complete.

steps.title: Reflect — artifacts
steps.body: Open both artifacts. In your journal write one sentence: “Since Day 1, the biggest change in my understanding is …” Be specific (tokens, reasoning, streaming, context)—not “I learned a lot.”
steps.why: Closure before Phase 1.
steps.outcome: Journal sentence saved.
steps.journalGuide:
Artifacts beat memory. day02-response.json captured your first structured chat response; day03-streaming.txt captured how streaming felt on the wire. Re-reading them after seven days shows how much mental model you built beyond copy-paste.

A good reflection names something you misunderstood on Day 1 that is obvious now—or something that is still fuzzy and needs Phase 1.

steps.title: Close Phase 0
steps.body: Mark Day 7 done. Celebrate bootstrap complete—Phase 1 adds SLM depth and a Python client.
steps.why: You can operate local lfm3 like a microservice.
steps.outcome: Phase 0 days show done in Daily progress when all steps complete.
